BOOK II.

<margin>Thus the idle crowd of servants can be excluded.</margin>
I return to the arrangement of the citizens. The eldest (as I have said) presides over the family. Wives serve their husbands, children serve their parents, and, in short, the younger serve their elders. Every city is divided into four equal parts. In the middle of each part is a marketplace for all types of goods. The products of every family are brought to certain houses there, and each species of item is distributed separately into warehouses. From these, any head of a family requests whatever he and his household need, and he takes what he asks for without money and without any payment at all. For why should anything be refused? Since there is an abundance of all things, there is no fear that anyone might want to demand more than is necessary. For why should one be thought to request what is superfluous when he is certain that he will never lack anything?

<sig>G 7</sig>

<summary>This passage describes the distribution of goods in an Utopian city, where resources are gathered in central marketplaces and provided freely to families according to need, eliminating the concept of money or scarcity.</summary>
<keywords>Utopia, social organization, marketplace, resource distribution, family structure, economic system</keywords>
